title: France’s long history of revolt
gist: A historian's eyewitness account of the October 2026 lycéen-led protests and the 17 October riots in France, set against a long French tradition of street protest; he argues this time the state is seen as impotent rather than oppressive, and the radicalisation benefits Mélenchon and especially the National Rally.

insights.claim: French street protest is explained by a highly centralised state with weak intermediary bodies such as low union membership, so direct action is seen as the only effective lever; the Devaquet (1986), Juppé (1995) and Villepin (2006) reforms were all withdrawn after protests.
insights.speaker: Julian Jackson
insights.so_what: Reform announcements in France carry a high withdrawal risk; fiscal consolidation under protest pressure should be discounted.
insights.quote: revolution does not make reforms but prevents them
insights.locator: The frequency of demonstrations has certainly increased

insights.claim: Protest frequency has risen since the Fifth Republic's founding in 1958, often ascribed to a stronger executive and weaker parliament closing off other channels, so street pressure became the main means of influencing the state.
insights.speaker: Julian Jackson
insights.so_what: Institutional design makes street politics a structural feature, not an anomaly.
insights.locator: The frequency of demonstrations has certainly increased

insights.claim: The 1995 anti-reform strikes against Juppé involved up to two million people at peak, and 1968 may have been the largest general strike in any advanced industrial society.
insights.speaker: Julian Jackson
insights.so_what: Historical benchmarks for sizing how disruptive current strike calls (CGT general strike 5 November) could become.
insights.locator: The number of French popular protest movements since 1900

themes.theme: The 2026 lycéen movement and 17 October riots

insights.claim: Unlike earlier protests against an overbearing state, the 2026 movement began from the sense of an impotent state, after Macron's 2024 dissolution produced no majority; the government voted its last budget after many months and has not yet voted the next.
insights.speaker: Julian Jackson
insights.so_what: Governance paralysis, not a specific reform, is the grievance, so concessions may not defuse it.
insights.locator: This does not fit the case of the recent movement of school students

insights.claim: Protests began over concrete school issues (dilapidated buildings, no heating, absent teachers, Parcoursup) at Lycée Saint-Exupéry in Créteil, then grew into a magnet for cost-of-living anger and contempt for Macron, drawing in teachers and energy workers on strike.
insights.speaker: Julian Jackson
insights.so_what: Energy-sector strikes are a possible operational and power-supply risk worth watching.
insights.locator: The current protest started in a lycée from a relatively deprived Paris suburb

insights.claim: More than 6,000 demonstrators, mostly minors, were taken into custody in a little over a week but only about a third faced charges, which the author reads as intimidation aimed at the far right; it backfired and further radicalised protesters.
insights.speaker: Julian Jackson
insights.so_what: Heavy-handed repression is escalating rather than containing unrest.
insights.locator: The government responded not by dialogue but repression

insights.claim: The 17 October demonstration was followed by rioting and looting across France, including the burning of Limoges town hall; casseurs from the banlieues mattered more than black bloc activists, about 2,400 arrests were made, and the Interior Minister offered his resignation, which Macron refused.
insights.speaker: Julian Jackson
insights.so_what: Shows state incapacity on public order, deepening the legitimacy theme in French politics.
insights.locator: Initially there was nothing unusual about that demonstration

insights.claim: Social media amplifies repression and disorder: TikTok plays the role radio played in 1968, feeding users divergent clips by algorithm, and small well-organised delinquent groups coordinated via social media outwitted the police.
insights.speaker: Julian Jackson
insights.so_what: Faster mobilisation and narrative fragmentation make unrest harder to predict and contain.
insights.locator: Even if the reality of repression has become less violent

insights.claim: Jackson sees 2026 as unlike 1968: it comes in a period of economic stagnation and morosity rather than growth and revolutionary optimism, leaving 'a void not a beach'.
insights.speaker: Julian Jackson
insights.so_what: Without optimism or a clear programme the unrest may be nihilistic and harder to resolve via negotiation.
insights.locator: Walking through the debris of broken glass

insights.claim: The unrest is radicalising French politics and squeezing the centre: Mélenchon has gained among the young while avoiding condemning the casseurs, Le Pen only needs to sound statesmanlike, and the centrist politicians have been inaudible.
insights.speaker: Julian Jackson
insights.so_what: Polarised extremes raise odds of a populist-dominated 2027 and policy unpredictability.
insights.locator: there is no doubt of its enduring political impact

insights.claim: Unlike 1968, which produced the biggest right-wing parliamentary majority in French history for the Gaullists, the beneficiary this time is the extreme-right National Rally because the Gaullist right hardly exists.
insights.speaker: Julian Jackson
insights.so_what: Order-restoration backlash likely favours the RN; consider French political risk premium into 2027.
insights.locator: The events of 1968 resulted in an election in June

insights.claim: Further mobilisation is scheduled: Gilets Jaunes protests on 24 and 31 October and a CGT general strike on 5 November, while the government has responded with curfews and bans on marches in many cities.
insights.speaker: Julian Jackson
insights.so_what: Near-term catalysts for French disruption and political headlines.
insights.locator: The Gilets Jaunes have called further protests

insights.claim: The Jordan Bardella antisemitic-comments story briefly set back the RN's detoxification effort but was overshadowed by the unrest.
insights.speaker: Julian Jackson
insights.so_what: RN reputational risks have been displaced by the order crisis.
insights.locator: Just as the lycée movement got under way, the RN seemed on the back foot
